bundle.name: Britain and Ireland: day-shaped playbooks
bundle.description: Eight days across London, Edinburgh, Skye, Bath and the Cotswolds, West Penwith, Eryri and County Clare. Built around the rules that actually decide whether a day works here — which market runs on which morning, which car park is gone by nine, which timed slot is both the cheapest and the best, and which stretch of coast is only there at low water.
sources: PROVENANCE: written without live web access (the session's search budget was spent and outbound fetches were blocked), so venue names, prices and opening rules come from model knowledge rather than pages read at authoring time. The URLs below are canonical references for those facts, NOT sources that were fetched and checked. Treat every price and time here as needing a verification pass before it is quoted as fact — see KI-2026-09-06-d.

playbooks.name: A Sunday on Columbia Road, then down Brick Lane
playbooks.summary: The East End on the one morning of the week it makes sense — flowers at eight, the Boundary Estate, the Truman yards, a salt beef beigel, and a candlelit house where nobody is allowed to speak.

sourceTrip.name: Ten days in London, mostly east

stops.title: Columbia Road Flower Market, first lap
stops.notes: Sunday only, roughly 08:00 to 15:00 — there is no market here on any other day of the week and the street is a row of shut shutters if you turn up on a Saturday. Be on it by 08:15: by 10:30 the road is a single shuffling file and you cannot turn round, let alone carry a tree. The buying rule is the reverse of the walking rule — do the first lap empty-handed, then come back at the end. After about 14:00 the traders would rather sell at a loss than load stock back onto the van, and the shouting starts. Nearest station is Hoxton on the Overground, not a tube; Bethnal Green and Old Street are both a ten-minute walk.

stops.title: Coffee and a slice in Ezra Street, behind the stalls

location.name: Ezra Street and Lily Vanilli Bakery

stops.notes: The yard off the middle of Columbia Road is where locals stand while the tourists queue on the street. Lily Vanilli is Sunday-only too, and sells out of the good things before noon. E Pellicci on Bethnal Green Road is the famous caff round here and it is shut on Sundays — plan a different morning for it rather than walking over and finding out.

stops.title: Arnold Circus and the Boundary Estate
stops.notes: Two minutes off Columbia Road and almost nobody makes the detour. The mound under the bandstand is the rubble of the slum that stood here, and the estate built on top of it in 1900 was the first council housing in the country. Free, takes twenty minutes, and it is the one thing on this day that explains the rest of it.

stops.title: Brick Lane: the Truman yards and the Backyard Market
stops.notes: Sunday is the only day all of the Brick Lane markets run together. Backyard Market is the vintage one and the Sunday UpMarket is food and makers; both are in the Truman Brewery yards on the west side, signposted badly. Skip the northern end of Brick Lane where the curry-house touts work the pavement — the good end is south of the railway bridge. Old Spitalfields Market is 400m west if this is too much of a crush.

stops.title: Salt beef beigel at Beigel Bake
stops.notes: There are two beigel shops within thirty metres and people argue about them permanently: the white-fronted one at 159 is Beigel Bake and open 24 hours, the yellow one at 155 is the older Beigel Shop. Order salt beef with mustard and pickle, say yes to both, and eat it standing up — there is nowhere to sit and never has been. The queue moves faster than it looks because there is only one thing to order.

stops.title: Dennis Severs House, by candle
stops.notes: Book the timed slot in advance — it is a private house with about a dozen people in it at a time and walk-ups are turned away. Silence is genuinely enforced and so is the no-photographs rule; if that sounds like a gimmick, it is the entire point, and it stops working the moment somebody talks. The candlelit Silent Night sittings are the ones to want. Not for children, and not for anyone who wants a guide to explain things.

stops.title: A pint at The Carpenters Arms
stops.notes: A back-street pub the Kray twins once bought for their mother, now simply a very good one — long beer list, no music loud enough to shout over. It is a five-minute walk north from Brick Lane up Cheshire Street, which on a Sunday is still half a market itself. If it is rammed, The Royal Oak on the corner of Columbia Road does the same job and puts you back where the day started.

playbooks.name: The Wallace, a matinee, and a tasting menu on the Strand
playbooks.summary: One deliberately expensive London day done in the right order — a free museum nobody queues for in the morning, a mid-week matinee, and a two-star kitchen at eight, with a room booked so the last course is not spent watching the clock.

stops.title: Daunt Books and Marylebone High Street
stops.notes: The Edwardian galleried room at the back is the reason to come, and it is shelved by country rather than by genre, so the novels, histories and guidebooks for one place stand together. Go before 10:30 and you get it nearly empty. If it is a Sunday, the Marylebone farmers market runs in the Cramer Street car park behind Waitrose — worth ten minutes.

stops.title: The Wallace Collection
stops.notes: Free, open every day from 10:00, and ten minutes from Oxford Street with none of the crowd. The terms of the bequest forbid anything leaving or joining the collection, which means nothing here ever travels to a blockbuster show somewhere else — you see it in this house or not at all. Everyone stops at the Laughing Cavalier and the Fragonard and then leaves; the arms and armour in the basement is one of the best collections in Europe and is usually empty.

stops.title: Lunch at The Golden Hind
stops.notes: A 1914 fish-and-chip room on a lane that kinks the way the old river did. Eat light — dinner tonight is four hours long. It is a short lunch service and it fills with local office workers from about 12:30, so go straight after the museum rather than wandering. Bring-your-own-wine at dinner only, no corkage nonsense at lunch.

stops.title: Across to Covent Garden
stops.notes: Twenty-five minutes on foot down through Mayfair, or two stops on the Jubilee and Piccadilly with a change at Green Park — the walk is faster than it looks and far more pleasant. Tap in and out with the same card; there is no need for a paper ticket or an Oyster any more.

stops.title: West End matinee, stalls
stops.notes: Matinees are Wednesday and Saturday almost everywhere, usually 14:00 or 14:30 — a Monday or Tuesday afternoon in the West End has nothing on at all, which catches people out. Book direct with the theatre rather than a reseller, and check the seating plan for the specific house: many of these are Victorian buildings where the front of the dress circle beats the back of the stalls for the same money. TKTS in Leicester Square sells genuine same-day discounts if you are willing to take what is left.

stops.title: A drink in the American Bar at The Savoy
stops.notes: No reservations, so the trick is to arrive before 18:00 — after that there is a queue in the lobby and it does not move. One cocktail costs what a bottle costs elsewhere and you are paying for the room and the piano, which is a fair trade once. Dress is smart; no sportswear, and they mean it. Beaufort Bar across the hall takes bookings if you would rather not gamble.

stops.title: Ikoyi, tasting menu with the pairing
stops.notes: Two stars, one menu, no choices, and it is West African larder cooking rather than anything you can predict from the address. Reservations open on a rolling window and the good times go in minutes — set an alarm for the release rather than trying your luck. The pairing roughly doubles the bill and is the part people regret skipping; a half-pairing is usually available if you ask when booking rather than at the table. Three and a half hours is the honest length, which is why the theatre is a matinee and not an evening show.

stops.title: A room on Aldwych rather than a night bus
stops.notes: The single decision that makes the rest of the day work: after a pairing you are not driving, and the last trains out of the centre would have you leaving before the final course. Rates on a Tuesday or Wednesday are routinely a third below Friday and Saturday, so a mid-week matinee is cheaper twice over. Two minutes on foot from the restaurant and about six from the theatres.

playbooks.name: Arthur's Seat at dawn, the Old Town, and a dram on the West Bow
playbooks.summary: A hill, a castle and a closed street underground, done in the order that beats the crowds at all three — then the best whisky bar in the city, which has no music, no cocktails and no interest in your opinion.

stops.title: Arthur's Seat from the Palace car park
stops.notes: 251m, free, no ticket and no gate, and about forty minutes up if you are moving. Three things people get wrong. The Radical Road under Salisbury Crags has been closed since a 2018 rockfall and is still fenced — do not plan a route through it. The Gutted Haddie, the eroded gully straight up the west face, is a scramble that turns to mud and is where the ankle injuries come from; take the made path from the Palace car park or the Queen's Drive. And if the forecast is bad, drive round to Dunsapie Loch, which cuts the climb to twenty minutes from a car park most visitors never find. It is a marked hold because the summit is genuinely dangerous in a Forth gale — the wind is roughly double what it is at the bottom.

stops.title: Coffee and a bacon roll before the Royal Mile wakes up
stops.notes: The lower Royal Mile below the World's End is the quiet half and stays that way until about eleven. Walk up rather than taking a bus: the Canongate closes and kirkyard are where the Old Town is still a place people live rather than a souvenir corridor.

stops.title: Edinburgh Castle, first slot after opening
stops.notes: Timed entry, booked online in advance, and cheaper online than at the gate — the gate queue on the esplanade can be forty minutes in summer for the privilege of paying more. Go straight up to the Crown Room and St Margaret's Chapel first and work back down; everyone else does the sequence in the printed order and bunches at the top by noon. The One O'Clock Gun is fired every day except Sunday, Good Friday and Christmas Day, and if you want it you need to still be here at 13:00, which this day is not.

stops.title: A hog roast roll from Oink on Victoria Street
stops.notes: A whole pig in the window and three decisions: roll size, haggis or not, and apple sauce or chilli. Six quid and five minutes, which is the point on a day with a booked slot at 13:30. Take it down the curve of Victoria Street and eat it in the Grassmarket looking back up at the castle rock.

stops.title: The Real Mary King's Close

location.name: The Real Mary King's Close, 2 Warriston's Close

stops.notes: A genuine 17th-century street sealed under the City Chambers, and the only one of the Old Town underground attractions that is the real thing rather than a vault repurposed for a ghost act. Timed tours in small groups, booked ahead, and they do sell out. It is cold and low — you will duck. The costumed guiding is hammier than it needs to be; the archaeology under it is not.

stops.title: The Bow Bar, and a shelf you have not tried
stops.notes: Several hundred bottles behind the bar, no music, no television and no cocktails — the room is built for conversation and the staff will talk you through a region for as long as you like if you are not in a hurry. Ask for something you cannot buy at home rather than the name you already know; the independent bottlings on the top shelves are the reason to be here. Order a half measure and water on the side. If it is full, Kay's Bar off Jamaica Street in the New Town is fifteen minutes downhill and is the other answer to the same question.

stops.title: Dinner at The Gardener's Cottage

location.name: The Gardener's Cottage, 1 Royal Terrace Gardens

stops.notes: A gardener's cottage in the London Road gardens with two long communal tables and a set menu that changes daily — you sit next to strangers and there is no choosing, which is either the charm or the dealbreaker. Book weeks out; there are about thirty covers. It is a twenty-minute walk from the Old Town round the back of Calton Hill, which is the pleasant way to end up back where the hill was this morning.

playbooks.name: Trotternish end to end, with somebody else driving
playbooks.summary: The Storr, the Quiraing and the Fairy Glen in one loop out of Portree — with a shared driver-guide, because Skye's single-track roads and its car parks are the two things that ruin this day when you do it yourself.

stops.title: Picked up in Portree, north on the A855
stops.notes: A private driver-guide for the day is roughly the cost of the car divided by however many of you there are — split four ways it is comparable to hiring a car and cheaper than hiring one badly. What you are actually buying is the parking problem going away and somebody who knows which passing place to sit in. The one rule visitors break constantly on Skye: passing places are for passing, not for photographs, and a car parked in one on the Staffin road blocks the whole glen.

stops.title: The Old Man of Storr before the car park goes
stops.notes: Pay-and-display, and in June to August it is full by about nine — after that people park on the verge and get ticketed, because the roadside is now enforced along that whole stretch. The path is rebuilt and good underfoot, 2.3 miles return, an hour and a half at a stroll, but the last pull to the pinnacles is loose and the whole thing is inside cloud on roughly half the mornings of the year, which is why this is a hold rather than a plan. If the top is grey, the lower viewpoint still works and you have not wasted the morning.

stops.title: Lealt Gorge and Kilt Rock

location.name: Kilt Rock and Mealt Falls viewpoint

stops.notes: Two roadside stops fifteen minutes apart, ten minutes each, free. Kilt Rock is the one on every postcard — a waterfall going straight off a basalt cliff into the sea. Stand at the fence for thirty seconds and listen: the railings hum in the wind, which is a genuinely strange noise and the thing people remember. Lealt, just south, has the better short walk and a quarter of the people.

stops.title: The Quiraing, out and back to the Table

location.name: Quiraing car park, Staffin to Uig road

stops.notes: The road up from Staffin is single-track with a one-in-four climb and a car park that is a field — it is full by 09:30 in season and there is nowhere else. The full circuit gets described as a loop, but the high return leg above the landslip is badly eroded and has been partly closed more than once; the honest version is the level traverse out to the Prison and the Table and back the way you came, which is the good half anyway. Two hours, mostly flat, with one exposed slabby step that is unpleasant in the wet.

stops.title: Lunch at the top of the peninsula
stops.notes: A tiny coffee-and-cake place in a shed at the far north end, open seasonally and closed on days the owners decide it is — check before you commit the drive. The Columba 1400 cafe in Staffin is the reliable fallback and does proper soup. There is nothing else between here and Uig, so eat when the chance appears rather than when you are hungry.

stops.title: The Fairy Glen above Uig
stops.notes: Free, no ticket, a strange miniature landscape of grass cones about a mile up a side road from Uig. Two things worth knowing: do not build stone spirals, because the crofters and the ranger service clear them every week and the practice is stripping the soil; and this is not the Fairy Pools, which are in Glen Brittle forty miles the other way with a car park that is full by nine. Confusing the two is the most common wasted afternoon on Skye — the Pools are a different day, and one that starts early.

stops.title: Skye Museum of Island Life at Kilmuir
stops.notes: Seven thatched blackhouses kept as a croft township, run by the family whose township it was. Cheap, seasonal, usually shut by 17:00 and all day Sunday out of high season — this is the stop to drop if the Quiraing overran. Flora MacDonald's grave is in the cemetery on the headland just above, five minutes on foot, and the view from it back down the Minch is the better half of the stop.

stops.title: Dinner at Scorrybreac, Portree
stops.notes: About twenty covers in a room over the harbour, one sitting, set menu, and it books out weeks ahead in summer — reserve before you book anything else on Skye. If you miss it, Sea Breezes on the quay does the shellfish plainly and takes walk-ins earlier in the evening. Portree stops serving food remarkably early for a town this size; anything after 21:00 means a bar meal or nothing.

playbooks.name: Bath in one day: the Baths at opening, two villages, the roof pool at dusk
playbooks.summary: A deliberately indulgent Bath day built round two timed tickets and one drive — the Roman Baths before the coaches, Castle Combe and Lacock in the afternoon light, and the thermal roof pool with the Abbey lit behind it.

stops.title: Paddington to Bath Spa on the 08:00
stops.notes: About ninety minutes on the fast service and the station is a five-minute walk from the Abbey, which is why this works as a day at all. Advance singles released twelve weeks out are a third of the walk-up fare — booking on the morning is the single most expensive mistake available in British travel. Sit on the left going down for the Avon valley. Anything later than the 08:00 puts you into the Roman Baths behind the coach parties, and the whole shape of this day depends on not being.

stops.title: The Roman Baths, first hour

location.name: The Roman Baths, Abbey Church Yard

stops.notes: Timed entry, booked online, and the price moves with the slot — weekday mornings are the cheapest and the emptiest at once. Take a slot before 10:00: the coaches from London and Stonehenge arrive between 11:00 and 14:00 and the Great Bath terrace becomes unusable. The water is 46 degrees, untreated and genuinely unsafe to touch, which is what the signs are actually about. The included audio guide has a separate Bill Bryson commentary track that is better company than the official one. Do not drink the spa water in the Pump Room unless you want to know what it tastes like, which is the only reason anyone does.

stops.title: Bath Abbey and a Sally Lunn bun

location.name: Bath Abbey and Sally Lunn's, North Parade Passage

stops.notes: The Abbey asks a donation at the door and the fan vaulting is worth it; the tower tours are separate, limited and go up 212 steps to the roof if you have booked one. Sally Lunn's is round the corner in one of the oldest houses in the city and the bun is a brioche the size of a plate — order one between two, savoury half then sweet half, or you will not want dinner. The cellar kitchen museum downstairs is free if you are eating.

stops.title: The Circus, the Royal Crescent and No.1
stops.notes: Walk up Gay Street so the Circus arrives suddenly, which is how it was designed to. The lawn in front of the Royal Crescent is public and you can lie on it; the ha-ha at the bottom is the trick that makes the park look like it belongs to the houses. No.1 is the end house done out as it was in the 1770s and takes forty-five minutes. If you are short of time this is the stop to cut — the exterior is the thing.

stops.title: Out to Castle Combe and Lacock
stops.notes: Half a day with a car and driver, shared, which is what a group of three or four should do here — the villages are twenty minutes apart and forty from Bath, and the bus connections between them are effectively fictional. Castle Combe has no parking in the village at all: the car park is up on the hill by the main road and you walk five minutes down, which is also the best way to see it. Lacock is owned end to end by the National Trust and the street is free to walk; the Abbey and the Fox Talbot museum are ticketed and stop admitting around 17:00, so do Castle Combe first. Neither village has a cash machine and Lacock's shops close early.

stops.title: Thermae Bath Spa, the rooftop at dusk

location.name: Thermae Bath Spa, Hot Bath Street

stops.notes: The only place in Britain where you can get into the natural thermal water, two minutes from the Roman ones you were not allowed to touch this morning. Book the two-hour session; robe, towel and slippers are included and hiring them separately is a needless extra. Last entry is two hours before closing and they are strict about it. Go up to the open-air rooftop pool in the last of the light with the Abbey floodlit over the parapet — that fifteen minutes is what the ticket is for. Over-16s only in most sessions, and it is busiest at weekends from about 14:00.

stops.title: Dinner at The Olive Tree

location.name: The Olive Tree, The Queensberry Hotel, Russel Street

stops.notes: Bath's starred kitchen, in the basement of a Georgian townhouse hotel five minutes from the Assembly Rooms. Book the tasting menu when you reserve rather than deciding at the table — they need the notice, and the a la carte is a lesser version of the same cooking. A late sitting after the spa is the right order: the reverse leaves you in a thermal pool feeling like a boiled dinner.

stops.title: Stay the night on the Crescent
stops.notes: Two houses in the middle of the Crescent with a garden behind that nobody walking past knows is there. The point of staying rather than taking the last train is the Crescent at seven in the morning with nobody on it — a completely different building from the one in every photograph. Midweek rates are well below Friday and Saturday, and Bath sells out entirely on rugby weekends and over the Christmas market.

playbooks.name: St Ives to Zennor on the coast path, then Porthcurno at low water
playbooks.summary: The hardest six miles of the South West Coast Path, a pub lunch at the far end of them, and a cliff theatre in the evening — with the tide table doing as much planning as you are.

stops.title: Leave the car at St Erth, take the branch line in
stops.notes: St Ives in August is a town with three car parks and about four thousand cars looking for them; Trenwith fills by 09:30 and the queue down into the town does not move. The branch line from St Erth is twelve minutes along the Hayle estuary and over Carbis Bay, all-day parking at the station is a few pounds, and it is one of the best short railway rides in Britain. It runs every half hour and is the answer even in February. Cost here covers the day's car and the station parking.

stops.title: The coast path, St Ives to Zennor

location.name: South West Coast Path, St Ives Head to Zennor Head

stops.notes: Six and a half miles that people budget three hours for and take four and a half. This is the roughest stretch of the entire 630-mile path — boulder fields, chest-high bracken in late summer, granite that turns greasy the moment it rains, and no bail-out point and no water once you are past Pen Enys. Do it westbound so the wind is behind you and the pub is at the end. Marked as a hold because in a real Atlantic blow the exposed sections above Mussel Point are not sensible; the inland Coffin Path between the same two villages is the honest alternative and takes half the time. Tell the pub roughly when you expect to arrive and then ring when you are an hour out.

stops.title: Lunch at The Gurnard's Head
stops.notes: A mustard-yellow pub alone on the B3306 about a mile past Zennor — book, because it is the only kitchen for miles and it fills with people who drove. The bar menu comes out of the same kitchen for half the price of the dining room and is what to order after four hours of walking. They will keep a table if you call. The Tinners Arms in Zennor village itself is the shorter walk and does a decent pint and a plainer plate if you are done in.

stops.title: Across the peninsula to Porthcurno

location.name: B3306 and the A30 to Porthcurno

stops.notes: Half an hour by car, or the Land's End Coaster bus, which is an open-top double decker and does the whole coast road as a sightseeing trip that happens to be public transport. The B3306 is narrow with granite hedges either side and there is nowhere to pull in — if you are driving it, go slowly and be ready to reverse.

stops.title: Porthcurno beach on the falling tide
stops.notes: Check the Newlyn tide tables before you fix the time of this stop, and treat everything else in the afternoon as movable around it. At high water on a spring tide there is essentially no beach here — the sand is gone and the cove is a wall of surf against the rocks. On the ebb it opens into the white shell sand that made the place famous, and the walk round to Pedn Vounder appears at the eastern end. That crossing is cut off by the sea and people get stranded there every single summer; do not start it on a rising tide.

stops.title: The Minack Theatre
stops.notes: Daytime entry is timed and booked online, and on performance days the site closes to sightseers in the early afternoon — check the what's-on before you plan an afternoon here, because turning up to a locked gate is the standard Minack disappointment. If you are coming for a show instead, bring a cushion and a waterproof: the seats are concrete, performances go ahead in rain, and the wind off the sea at nine at night is colder than the day suggests. Parking is on site and small.

stops.title: Dinner at The Old Coastguard, Mousehole
stops.notes: Same owners as the Gurnard's Head, a terrace of palms above the water, and the fish is whatever came into Newlyn that morning. Book. Mousehole's harbour road is one car wide with no turning space and residents' permits on most of it — park in the car park at the top of the village and walk down the hill, which takes five minutes and saves an argument. The village is at its best out of season, and in late December it is lit up for the harbour lights and unbookable.

playbooks.name: Yr Wyddfa: up the Pyg, down the Miners', and a mug of tea in Llanberis
playbooks.summary: The Snowdon loop done from the park-and-ride instead of the car park you cannot book, starting early enough to have the ridge alone — with the slate town at the bottom given the afternoon it deserves.

stops.title: Nant Peris park-and-ride and the Sherpa bus up to Pen-y-Pass
stops.notes: Pen-y-Pass has about a hundred spaces, it is pre-book only, and the slots go weeks ahead in summer — driving up there on spec means driving back down again. Everyone local uses Nant Peris instead: cheap all-day parking at the bottom of the pass and the Sherpa'r Wyddfa S1 up the hill for a couple of pounds. Check the first departure the night before, because the timetable changes with the season and the early bus is the whole plan. Verges on the A4086 are double-yellowed and actively ticketed.

stops.title: Up the Pyg Track
stops.notes: Three and a half miles and about 720m of ascent — the shortest way up because Pen-y-Pass already sits at 359m. Leaving at 07:30 buys you two hours before the path turns into a queue at the zigzags. Crib Goch branches left near the start and is not an alternative route: it is a grade one scramble along a knife edge with three hundred metres of air either side, and it accounts for a large share of the mountain rescue call-outs in Eryri. Read the Met Office mountain forecast, not the town forecast — the summit is in cloud roughly two days in three and it can be fifteen degrees colder up there with winds three times the valley speed. Hence a hold: if the forecast is wrong, the Miners' Track to Glaslyn and back is a fine day on its own.

stops.title: The summit and Hafod Eryri
stops.notes: 1,085m, the highest point in Wales, and there is a cafe in it — but Hafod Eryri only opens when the Snowdon Mountain Railway is running, roughly late March to the end of October and not at all if the trains are stopping short at Clogwyn in high wind. Outside that it is a locked stone building and a summit cairn, so carry lunch regardless. Queue for the trig point on one side and take the view from the other; almost nobody walks the two minutes to the quiet end of the platform.

stops.title: Down the Miners' Track past Glaslyn and Llyn Llydaw
stops.notes: Up one and down the other makes a proper loop back to the same bus stop, which is the reason to do it this way round rather than out and back. The Miners' drops steeply for the first twenty minutes to Glaslyn and then flattens into an old copper-mine track that is kind to tired knees for the last two miles. The causeway across Llyn Llydaw is the photograph everyone else took from above without knowing they could stand on it. The ruined barracks by Glaslyn are worth five minutes.

stops.title: The S1 back down the pass
stops.notes: The Sherpa runs on through to Llanberis, so you can stay on past your car, spend the afternoon in the town and pick the bus back up to Nant Peris in the evening. Buses fill from the Pen-y-Pass end in the afternoon and standing is not allowed on the mountain road — if two go past full, walking down the old road to Nant Peris takes about fifty minutes and is pleasant.

stops.title: Pete's Eats
stops.notes: The climbers' cafe at the centre of British mountaineering for fifty years — bright walls, a wall of route guides and logbooks you are meant to read, and mugs of tea that hold a pint because that is what people coming off a hill want. Enormous portions and cheap. Cash still gets a warmer reception than a card. Upstairs has the weather forecasts pinned up, which is how everyone here decides tomorrow.

stops.title: The National Slate Museum and Dolbadarn Castle

location.name: National Slate Museum, Padarn Country Park

stops.notes: Free entry, in the workshops of the Dinorwig quarry that hangs above the town — the slate landscape of northwest Wales became a World Heritage Site in 2021 and this is the room that explains why. The slate-splitting demonstration is the best twenty minutes in Llanberis and runs only a few times a day, so check the board when you arrive rather than wandering in at closing. Dolbadarn Castle is a ten-minute walk round the lake, a single Welsh round tower from the 1200s, free and open.

stops.title: Pizza and a pint at Gallt y Glyn
stops.notes: A bunkhouse pub at the Caernarfon end of the village that has fed walkers pizza and local beer for years — no ceremony, no booking, and the room is entirely people who were on a mountain today. The Heights in the middle of the village is the busier alternative with live music some nights. Kitchens here stop early; anything after 21:00 in Llanberis is a bag of crisps.

playbooks.name: The Burren in the morning, the Cliffs of Moher at six
playbooks.summary: County Clare done backwards on purpose — limestone and a dolmen while everyone else is queueing at the cliffs, and the cliffs themselves in the evening light after the coaches have gone.

sourceTrip.name: The Wild Atlantic Way, south to north

stops.title: The R480 from Ballyvaughan over Corkscrew Hill
stops.notes: The whole trick of this day is direction. Every coach out of Galway does the Cliffs of Moher first, at eleven, and then the Burren; going the other way round means empty limestone all morning and empty cliffs all evening. Corkscrew Hill climbs out of Ballyvaughan in a set of hairpins built as famine relief work, and the pull-in at the top looks back over the whole bay. Fuel up before you leave the coast — there is nothing on the R480.

stops.title: Poulnabrone Dolmen
stops.notes: An OPW site with no gate, no ticket and no opening hours — you park across the road and walk out over the pavement. Roughly 5,800 years old, and the excavation found the remains of more than thirty people under it. The car park is small and the Galway coaches reach it around eleven, so this is a stop that is either sublime or a crowd depending entirely on whether you got here first. Walk out onto the clints and grikes away from the tomb: the flora in the cracks is the actual wonder of the Burren, Arctic and Mediterranean plants growing side by side, and it peaks in May and June.

stops.title: Caherconnell fort and the sheepdogs
stops.notes: A ring fort a kilometre south of the dolmen, still being excavated, on the family's own land. The sheepdog demonstrations run at fixed times a few times a day and are the reason to come — build the late morning around the one you want rather than turning up and hoping. Fort and dogs are sold together or separately and the combined ticket is the better value. Seasonal: much reduced from November to March, so check before making it the anchor of a winter day.

stops.title: The Burren Perfumery tea room at Carran
stops.notes: Free to walk into, at the end of a boreen you will be certain is the wrong turning — keep going. The tea room is garden vegetables, brown bread and cake, it is small, and it shuts earlier in the day than the perfumery does, so eat first and browse after. Cash is easier than card out here and the mobile signal is nil.

stops.title: Late lunch at the Wild Honey Inn
stops.notes: The first pub in Ireland to hold a Michelin star, and still a pub — you eat in the bar. It does not serve every day of the week and the days change with the season, so ring rather than assume; a closed Wild Honey with no plan B is a long drive to a chip van. Book if you can. Lisdoonvarna is otherwise a spa town that spends September being the matchmaking festival, which is a very different experience of the same street.

stops.title: Under the cliffs from Doolin pier
stops.notes: An hour-long cruise that runs south under the cliff face and turns at Hag's Head. You do not understand that the cliffs are 214m high until you are at the bottom of them looking up, and the sea stack and the nesting ledges are invisible from the top. Sailings are cancelled outright in any real swell and the decision is made on the morning, which is why this is a hold and why the evening plan needs to survive without it. Take the seasickness advice seriously — the Atlantic here is rarely flat.

stops.title: The Cliffs of Moher, evening slot
stops.notes: Entry is pre-booked and timed, priced by slot, and walk-ups are not guaranteed a space — the late slots are both the cheapest and by a distance the best. Three reasons the evening wins: the cliffs face west, so at noon you are looking at a wall in its own shadow and after five they are lit end to end; the coach fleet has gone by about half five; and the site stays open past the visitor centre's hours in summer. When you get up top, turn south towards Hag's Head rather than north to O'Brien's Tower, and within ten minutes you will have the cliff path more or less to yourself. Stay behind the wall — the grass edge is undercut and the wind here comes up the face.

stops.title: A session at Gus O'Connor's
stops.notes: Doolin has three session pubs within four hundred metres — O'Connor's in Fisherstreet, McGann's and McDermott's up in Roadford — and the honest advice is to look in all three. If one is a coach-party crush the other two will not be. Sessions start when the players arrive, which is nearer 21:45 than the time chalked on the board, and the first half hour is the tuning. Do not talk over a slow air; nobody will tell you to stop and everybody will notice.
